passage:
On Sunday night, in their Mumbai flat, Vaibhav sat on the bed and repeated the Hindi poem forty times for Monday's recitation. By ten o'clock the words came out smoothly. "Done!" Vaibhav told Indu didi.
On Monday the recitation went well.
On Friday the teacher said, "Surprise! Say it again for parents' day." Vaibhav stood up, said the first line and froze. The rest had gone, like chalk wiped off a board.
At home Indu didi smiled. "When I learn poems, I say them for ten minutes a day, for five days. It feels slow, but they stay."
Vaibhav frowned, then took the book out again. "Ten minutes. Starting today."

qa.q: How many times did Vaibhav repeat the poem on Sunday night?
qa.a: Vaibhav repeated it forty times.

qa.q: Why did Vaibhav feel "Done!" on Sunday night?
qa.a: Vaibhav felt confident and relieved because the words were coming out smoothly by ten o'clock, so the poem felt learned, even though it had all been packed into one evening.

qa.q: What does Indu didi suggest, and why does it work better?
qa.a: Ten minutes a day for five days; spreading it out makes the poem stay, even if it feels slower.

qa.q: What might the teacher think on seeing Vaibhav freeze on Friday?
qa.a: The teacher may be surprised, since Monday went well, and may guess the poem was crammed rather than truly learned.

grounding: It shows a child who learns a poem in one evening, recites it the next day and loses it within days.

passage:
"Himani, dinner!"
"One more time, Mummy. I'll say the poem fifty times tonight."
"The competition is next week."
"I'll learn it all tonight, so I'm free after."
Three days later:
"Say it for Nani on the phone, Himani."
"'The river runs...' um. 'The river runs...' Mummy, it's gone!"
"All of it?"
"Only the first line is left." Himani's lip wobbled.
Sarita, her mother, sat down beside her. "Remember when I learned the road signs for my driving test? A few every night for a week, and I still know them."
"So... a little every day?"
"A little every day. And tomorrow, try saying it before you open the book."
Himani wiped her eyes. "Okay. Five minutes tonight."

qa.q: What was all that was left of the poem after three days?
qa.a: Only the first line was left.

qa.q: Why did Himani want to learn the whole poem in one night?
qa.a: Himani wanted to be free for the rest of the week, and saying it fifty times in one night felt like it would lock it in.

qa.q: What small step did Himani and Sarita agree on?
qa.a: Five minutes a day, trying to say the poem before opening the book.

qa.q: How might Sarita feel watching Himani's lip wobble?
qa.a: Sarita probably feels sympathy and wants to help rather than scold, which is why she shares her own road-sign story.

grounding: It shows a child who crams a poem in one evening and loses it within days, then tries learning a little each day.

passage:
Last year I thought I was a poem champion. The night before the recitation, I read the river poem over and over till midnight. Next morning I said every line perfectly.
A week later Arohi asked me to say it with her for fun. I got two lines in and stopped. Arohi, who had practised a little every day for two weeks, went all the way to the end.
I was annoyed, but I asked her how. She said, "I just said it at breakfast and at bedtime. Small bits."
This year, for the new poem, I tried her way. Ten minutes every evening. Last week I said it for my Nana, a whole month after the recitation. I'm Hansa, and I'm still a little proud.

qa.q: How long did Hansa read the poem the night before the recitation?
qa.a: Hansa read it over and over till midnight.

qa.q: Why was Hansa annoyed when Arohi finished the poem?
qa.a: Hansa had felt like a poem champion after a perfect recitation, so forgetting it a week later while Arohi remembered it felt unfair.

qa.q: What choice did Hansa make for the new poem, and what happened?
qa.a: Hansa tried Arohi's way, ten minutes every evening, and could still say it for Nana a whole month later. 🎉

qa.q: How might Arohi feel when Hansa asks how she did it?
qa.a: Arohi may feel pleased to share a simple trick, and glad Hansa asked instead of staying annoyed.

grounding: It shows a child whose poem, crammed in one night, faded within a week, while a friend's daily practice lasted.

passage: Class teacher's note, Class 4B, Tamarind Road School. Kavitha (age 9) was chosen to recite a poem at Friday's assembly. On Monday morning she said all sixteen lines to me without one mistake. She told me proudly she had learned the whole thing in one evening, "saying it again and again till dinner." On Thursday, at the practice, she stopped after line four. She tried twice more and her lip trembled. "But Miss, I knew it!" she said. I believe she did, on Monday. I took the poem and cut it into four strips of four lines. We agreed she would say one strip each morning with her Amma, and the next strip the day after, then all of them at the end of the week. The assembly moved to next Friday. I'll write again then. — Shalini

qa.q: How many lines did Kavitha say without a mistake on Monday morning?
qa.a: She said all sixteen lines without one mistake.

qa.q: What was Kavitha feeling when she said, "But Miss, I knew it!"
qa.a: She felt confused and upset 😢 because the poem had felt solid on Monday, so losing it by Thursday seemed unfair.

qa.q: What new plan did Shalini make, and why might it work better than one long evening?
qa.a: Splitting the poem into strips and practising one each morning spreads the learning over days, so it has time to settle instead of fading.

qa.q: How might Kavitha's Amma be part of the change?
qa.a: Amma becomes the morning practice partner, so learning becomes a small daily habit at home rather than one tiring night.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a child who learned a poem in one evening losing it within days, and a plan to spread practice out.

passage:
Wednesday
Dear diary, I am so annoyed. On Saturday night I learned the whole poem for the annual day audition. I said it twenty times, maybe thirty. I was perfect. Nani clapped.
Today at lunch Sumit said, "Test?" and held the paper. I did the first verse fine. Then my brain went white, like a blank board. Sumit had to whisper the middle lines. HOW?? It was all inside my head on Saturday!
Nani says learning is like watering her tulsi plant. If you pour a whole bucket once, most of it runs out. A little every day stays. I think she might be right, which is also annoying.
The audition is on Monday. I'm going to say one verse at breakfast, one at bedtime, and let Sumit test me in the bus every day.
Mridul

qa.q: When did Mridul learn the whole poem?
qa.a: On Saturday night, for the annual day audition.

qa.q: How can you tell Mridul felt frustrated about forgetting?
qa.a: Mridul writes "I am so annoyed" and "HOW??", and remembers being perfect on Saturday, which makes the blank feel unfair.

qa.q: What plan did Mridul choose for the days before Monday?
qa.a: Saying one verse at breakfast and one at bedtime, and letting Sumit test on the bus every day, which spreads the practice out.

qa.q: What might it be like for Sumit to whisper the middle lines?
qa.a: Sumit is trying to help a friend and may feel a bit awkward, but also useful, and now gets to be the daily tester.

grounding: A child's diary shows a poem learned in one evening fading within days, and a new plan to practise a little each day.
